bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Seasonality and weather dependence concentrated in a single dominant product line — Management names 'Seasonality Risk' explicitly: the Room AC segment is highly seasonal and vulnerable to volatile and unpredictable weather patterns, and 'unexpected shifts in weather patterns, fluctuating temperatures, or irregular seasonal changes make it challenging for air conditioning businesses to predict consumer demand accurately... leading to volatility in product sales and inventory misalignment.' This is not theoretical - the Directors' Report concedes FY2025-26 demand 'got adversely impacted owing to weather conditions' and the RAC industry stayed largely flattish. With Consumer Durables at 69% of divisional revenue and air conditioners and components accounting for over 90% of standalone turnover per BRSR, one weather season can swing the majority of the group. The stated mitigation is structural rather than operational - diversifying the mix into Electronics and Railway Subsystems & Defence to reduce dependence on RAC seasonality.
- OEM/ODM customer dependence - quality or delivery failure means loss of approved-vendor status, not just a penalty — The BRSR materiality table frames product quality and safety as 'non-negotiable': customers embed stringent quality specifications, dimensional tolerances and reliability standards in supply agreements, and 'failure to consistently meet these standards results in rejections, chargebacks, and ultimately, delisting from approved vendor lists.' Because Amber is a B2B contract manufacturer with no consumer brand of its own, the customer relationship IS the franchise - quality performance is described as 'the primary differentiator in vendor selection and long-term contract retention.' The same exposure runs through ESG: OEM customers embedding Scope 3 emissions tracking and supplier carbon criteria could put approved-vendor status at risk if credible climate action cannot be demonstrated, and compliance failures by supply chain partners can cause disqualification by ESG-conscious customers.
- Commodity price and currency volatility against structurally thin margins — Management lists 'Commodity Price and Currency Fluctuations' as a threat: short-term unpredictability in global prices of copper, aluminium and crude derivatives challenges operating margins, compounded by currency depreciation, and sustained cost inflation could itself change customer purchasing behaviour in price-sensitive segments. The BRSR supply-chain row adds that raw material price spikes 'can significantly compress gross margins if not adequately managed through procurement strategy or contractual pass-through mechanisms with customers' - i.e. pass-through is a mechanism to be negotiated, not a given. The exposure is amplified by the business model: consolidated Operating EBITDA margin is disclosed at 8.0% and net profit margin at 1.9%, so a small input-cost shock consumes a large share of profit.
- Multi-tier supply chain concentration, import dependence and geopolitical disruption — Procurement risk is the longest entry in the risk-management table, spanning commodity price volatility, currency depreciation, inflationary cost pressures, trade policy uncertainty, geopolitical and regional instability, global supply chain disruptions and critical component availability. The BRSR row is blunter still: import dependency for certain specialty inputs adds foreign exchange and logistics risk, and 'concentration risk from sole source or limited source supply arrangements for critical inputs amplifies vulnerability to disruption.' The consequence is asymmetric because OEM customers run just-in-time inventory - a supply failure at Amber 'translates rapidly into customer line stoppages and contractual penalties.' Mitigations cited are supplier diversification and qualified alternates, safety stock for long-lead inputs, supplier financial and compliance assessment, and a digital procurement platform.
- Technology obsolescence and the cost of staying qualified as capability moves up the value chain — 'Coping with Changing Technology' is a named risk: rapid technological advancement and evolving product requirements may require continuous portfolio realignment, and the threats section warns that existing products, processes or capabilities may become 'less competitive over time.' This bites hardest in the Electronics pivot, where the company is simultaneously moving into multi-layer and HDI PCB manufacturing - technologies it does not yet operate at scale - and into industrial automation and power electronics through acquired entities. R&D is explicitly framed in the BRSR as the difference between being 'a development partner rather than a commodity supplier', so under-investment compresses both pricing and programme wins. Regulatory technology transitions compound this: the HFC phase-down roadmap for high-GWP refrigerants and tightening BEE energy-efficiency norms (revised Star Labelling effective January 2026) force product redesign on an externally set clock.
- Execution and integration risk across a rapid acquisition and greenfield capex programme - with a realised loss already on the record — In one year the group added 7 manufacturing facilities (3 via acquisition), took majority stakes in Power-One (60%), Shogini Technoarts (80%) and Israel-listed Unitronics (40.2% rising to 50.4%), merged Ever Electronics into IL JIN, and committed to ECMS-approved investment plans of Rs 991 Crore (Ascent Circuits), Rs 3,215 Crore (Ascent-K) and Rs 500 Crore (Shogini), all funded partly by an approximately Rs 1,000 Crore QIP and approximately Rs 1,750 Crore raised at IL JIN. Every one of the three major planned expansions is described only as 'expected to become operational in the coming periods' with no commissioning date, and the Yujin JV plant is built but cannot produce until RDSO approvals arrive - a regulatory gate outside the company's control. That capital-at-risk is not hypothetical: reported PAT fell year-on-year because of an exceptional one-off impairment of the investment (including loan) in Shivaliks Mercantile plus the share of JV loss, and Sidwal exited that 49% joint venture entirely on 30 March 2026.
- Dependence on government policy schemes for the economics of the expansion plan — Management describes the government's policy framework as 'a key catalyst of our expansion plan.' The three largest committed projects rest on approvals under the Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme, whose outlay was itself only raised from Rs 22,919 Crore to Rs 40,000 Crore in the Union Budget 2026-27, and the RAC value-addition thesis (20-25% rising to 75-80%) rests on the PLI scheme for white goods. Demand assumptions lean the same way - the GST cut on RACs from 28% to 18% effective September 2025, record Railway capex of Rs 2.93 lakh crore, defence indigenisation. Scheme conditions, disbursement timing or a change in policy priority would therefore hit both the return on the capex already committed and the demand pull assumed behind it.
- Competitive intensity and a largely contractual workforce with high turnover — Management flags 'Market Competition' - pressure from both well-established players and new entrants demanding continuous innovation and strategic positioning. Two structural workforce exposures sit alongside it in the BRSR data. First, of 14,023 workers only 2,379 are permanent, with 11,644 other-than-permanent; total workforce is 21,000+ including contractual labour, so a large share of manufacturing capacity depends on contract labour whose availability and cost are outside the payroll. Second, turnover is high - permanent employee turnover of 25.26% in FY2025-26 (32.49% in FY2024-25), which for a business whose moat is described as R&D and process capability is a retention risk on the very capability being built. The one-off provision of Rs 9 Crore on account of the New Labour Code shows the cost of labour-regulation change flowing straight to reported profit.

business.body: Amber Enterprises India Limited, together with its subsidiaries and joint ventures (the 'Amber Group'), makes finished products and components for other brands rather than selling under its own consumer brand. In Consumer Durables it supplies Complete Built Units (CBUs) of Room and Commercial Air Conditioners plus a wide range of RAC and non-RAC components (heat exchangers, motors, multi-flow condensers, copper tubing, sheet metal, plastic extrusion, vacuum forming and injection moulding, refrigerator case liners, washing-machine tub assemblies) to leading MNC and domestic appliance brands. The Electronics Division supplies EMS (PCB assembly and box build), bare PCBs, power electronics and industrial automation solutions to consumer electronics, automotive, telecom, aerospace and defence, energy and industrial customers, while the Railway Subsystems & Defence Division (through Sidwal) supplies HVAC systems, rolling-stock subsystems and precision cooling to railways, metros, RRTS, buses and defence. Revenue split by division in FY2025-26 was 69% Consumer Durables, 27% Electronics and 4% Railway Subsystems & Defence.

outlook.body:
- Three stated priorities for the next phase of growth: deepening backward integration, expanding manufacturing capabilities, and accelerating innovation-led growth through disciplined execution
- Diversify away from a single-product RAC dependency into Electronics and mobility-led segments, so that no one division's cycle (notably weather-driven RAC demand) dictates group performance
- Deepen backward integration in the RAC/Consumer Durables value chain, extending from CBUs into RAC and non-RAC components to hold cost competitiveness and wallet share with OEM customers
- Build the Electronics Division into a comprehensive electronics solutions provider spanning EMS (PCB-A and Box Build), bare PCBs, power electronics and industrial automation, expanding both horizontally into new avenues and vertically into deeper capability
- Scale bare PCB capability specifically - multi-layer capacity at Ascent Circuits and Shogini, and advanced HDI PCB capability at Ascent-K - targeting a product category described as remaining highly import-dependent
- Grow inorganically through targeted stake acquisitions and technology partnerships (Power-One for power electronics, Shogini for bare PCB, Unitronics for industrial automation, Korea Circuit for HDI) rather than building every capability organically
- Use government policy schemes (PLI for white goods, ECMS for electronic components, Make in India / Atmanirbhar Bharat) as the explicit catalyst for the expansion plan and capital deployment
- In Railway Subsystems & Defence, raise content per coach by broadening from HVAC and pantry systems into Doors, Gangways, Couplers, Driving Gears, Pantographs and Braking Systems
- Scale the Defence vertical through specialised precision cooling products for strategic applications
- Enter mobile phone manufacturing as a new product category via the OPPO manufacturing collaboration, while explicitly balancing high-margin/low-volume against low-margin/high-volume high-ROCE businesses
- In Commercial Air Conditioning, expand the Light Commercial AC portfolio through product innovation (inverter ductable range, One-Way Cassette ACs) and new customer additions
- Optimise the manufacturing footprint continuously - adding facilities while consolidating, discontinuing or relocating others rather than only adding capacity
- Retain earnings rather than distribute them, funding capex and acquisitions internally while preserving balance-sheet strength; supplement with equity raises at parent and subsidiary level
- Position at the intersection of India's manufacturing growth, electronics scale-up and infrastructure-led demand through a sharper focus on technology, localisation and multi-sector participation

outlook.body: Amber's FY2025-26 expansion story is overwhelmingly an Electronics-division story funded partly by two capital raises (approximately Rs 1,000 Crore QIP at the parent and approximately Rs 1,750 Crore of CCPS and equity at IL JIN Electronics). As on 31st March 2026 the Company and its group entities collectively operate 37 manufacturing facilities across India and internationally, of which 16 are operated directly by the Company and 21 by subsidiaries and group entities. During the year 7 new manufacturing facilities were added, including 3 acquired through acquisitions, while certain existing facilities were consolidated or discontinued and two units (at Plot No. 36, Sector 31, Kasna Industrial Area, Site-IV, Greater Noida and one further industrial plot) were relocated to other operational facilities as part of ongoing operational optimisation. Three major planned expansions are under implementation and 'expected to become operational in the coming periods': IL JIN Electronics is expanding its PCB Assembly unit at Gat No. 160-2 and 164-2, Pimple Jagtap Road, Bhima Koregaon, Tal. Shirur, Pune, Maharashtra; Ascent Circuits is building a Multi-Layer PCB unit at Plot No. 8, ELCOSEZ, Viswanthapuram, Hosur, Krishnagiri District, Tamil Nadu, where construction is progressing well, backed by an ECMS-approved investment plan of Rs 991 Crore; and Ascent-K Circuit (a JV with Korea Circuit) is building an HDI PCB unit at Plot No. 4, Sector 10, EMC 2.0, YEIDA near Jewar Airport, Gautam Buddha Nagar, Uttar Pradesh, on a 16-acre site, backed by an ECMS-approved investment plan of Rs 3,215 Crore, with the ground-breaking ceremony held in June 2026. Shogini Technoarts separately secured ECMS approval for a multi-layer PCB investment plan of Rs 500 Crore. Growth also came inorganically through IL JIN: a 60% majority stake in Bengaluru-based Power-One Micro Systems (power electronics - BESS, solar inverters, EV chargers, industrial UPS) in August 2025 under definitive agreements dated 27th June 2025; an 80% stake in Maharashtra-based PCB maker Shogini Technoarts in December 2025 (adding single-sided, double-sided, multi-layer, metal-clad and flex PCB capability); and a stake in Israel-listed Unitronics built from an initial 40.2% in October 2025 to 49.7% by year-end and 50.4% in April 2026, giving majority ownership and access to HMI, PLC, variable frequency drive and industrial-automation software. In Consumer Durables the Company augmented Room AC manufacturing capacity at Sri City, Andhra Pradesh during the year and expanded the Light Commercial AC portfolio (inverter ductable range, One-Way Cassette ACs). In Railway Subsystems & Defence, Sidwal's new greenfield facility is expected to significantly strengthen manufacturing capacity, and the Yujin Machinery joint-venture facility is ready with commercial production expected to commence upon securing the requisite RDSO approvals. On the sustainability side the climate action strategy includes expansion of on-site solar power capacity and evaluation of Power Purchase Agreements for green electricity, though no megawatt figure is given. Beyond the three named planned expansions, no commissioning dates, capacity additions in product units, or rupee capex quantum for the group as a whole are disclosed anywhere in this bundle.

outlook.body:
- RAC household penetration in India is around 12%, materially below comparable Asian markets - management frames this as a multi-decade runway and 'visible headroom'
- GST on Room Air Conditioners was cut from 28% to 18% effective September 2025, which management expects to enhance affordability, support first-time adoption among price-sensitive consumers and improve access to premium 5-star models
- Rising ambient temperatures, extended summer seasons and more frequent heatwaves are shifting cooling from a discretionary luxury to a necessity, accelerating both first-time adoption and the replacement cycle, and lengthening the seasonal selling window
- Middle-class expansion - middle-class and affluent consumers are expected to account for 93% of total consumer spending by 2036; households in the upper-middle and high income bands are projected to rise sharply by 2030/31
- Urbanisation - India's urban population grew from roughly 31% in 2011 to roughly 36% in 2025 and is projected to exceed 40% by 2030, with housing-society expansion in Tier II and III cities driving RAC installations
- Per capita GDP rising from about US$ 2,591 in 2024 to a projected US$ 2,812 by 2026 and US$ 4,047 by 2030, crossing the affordability threshold for first-time and multi-room air conditioning
- PLI Scheme for white goods expected to bring cumulative investment of Rs 11,198 Crore across the value chain, with domestic value addition targeted to rise from 20-25% to 75-80%
- BEE revised Star Labelling standards implemented January 2026 mandate higher energy-performance benchmarks, strengthening demand for energy-efficient RACs and, by implication, for redesigned components
- FY2025-26 RAC demand was adversely impacted by non-conducive weather, but management insists the structural fundamentals remain firmly intact - an explicit demand-timing versus demand-structure distinction
- ESDM/EMS is maturing from pure assembly towards component engineering and value-added activity, with Indian manufacturers pushing import substitution and deeper local value addition
- ECMS outlay increased from an initial Rs 22,919 Crore to Rs 40,000 Crore in the Union Budget 2026-27, expected to attract investment commitments exceeding Rs 1.15 lakh crore, generate production worth over Rs 10 lakh crore and create more than 1.4 lakh direct jobs
- Rising electronics content per product and the growth of smart and connected devices expands EMS demand across sectors
- Automotive electronics and the EV ecosystem structurally increase electronic content per vehicle (telematics, connectivity, security, infotainment, powertrain electrification); rigorous qualification protocols create a high entry threshold that favours incumbents
- Digitalisation, cloud computing, digital services and data centres drive demand for electronic hardware, networking equipment and power management solutions
- Bare PCBs remain substantially import-dependent, which management presents as the localisation opportunity behind the Ascent/Ascent-K/Shogini investments
- Indian Railways allocated a record capital expenditure of Rs 2.93 lakh crore, with seven new high-speed rail corridors planned and continued Vande Bharat and Amrit Bharat deployment
- Vande Bharat Sleeper and Metro variants have more demanding climate-control requirements, driving higher technological complexity and higher value per coach in rail HVAC
- India's operational metro network crossed the 1,000-km milestone across 11 states and 23 cities - third largest in the world - with Metro and RRTS expansion across more than 20 cities unlocking multi-year subsystem demand
- Public-private partnership models in station redevelopment, rolling stock and logistics, alongside Make in India localisation, are broadening the addressable rail market
- Margin lever cited: operating EBITDA growth driven by improved operating performance and a favourable shift towards higher-margin products
- Mix lever cited: Consumer Durables provides a strong and growing baseline while the strategic shift towards electronics and mobility-led segments progressively reshapes the composition of the business
- Management's stated view is that manufacturers with integrated capabilities, strong technology partnerships and diversified product portfolios are best positioned to benefit from the shift to value-added electronics manufacturing - a self-description of Amber's positioning
- Railway Subsystems & Defence Division: 'The Division continued to witness encouraging momentum across the Railway, Metro, and Defence segments, supported by an expanding product portfolio and healthy order book visibility.'
- Chairman's statement on the same division: 'With a healthy order book and an expanding product portfolio, we remain optimistic about the strong growth prospects of this Division.'
- Railways outlook: 'With a broadening product portfolio and ramping offtake of products, the Company is strongly positioned to drive sustainable future growth.'
- No order-book value, tenure or book-to-bill figure is disclosed anywhere in this bundle - the mentions are qualitative only, and are confined to the Railway Subsystems & Defence Division

risks.note: Management names 'Seasonality Risk' explicitly: the Room AC segment is highly seasonal and vulnerable to volatile and unpredictable weather patterns, and 'unexpected shifts in weather patterns, fluctuating temperatures, or irregular seasonal changes make it challenging for air conditioning businesses to predict consumer demand accurately... leading to volatility in product sales and inventory misalignment.' This is not theoretical - the Directors' Report concedes FY2025-26 demand 'got adversely impacted owing to weather conditions' and the RAC industry stayed largely flattish. With Consumer Durables at 69% of divisional revenue and air conditioners and components accounting for over 90% of standalone turnover per BRSR, one weather season can swing the majority of the group. The stated mitigation is structural rather than operational - diversifying the mix into Electronics and Railway Subsystems & Defence to reduce dependence on RAC seasonality.
risks.risk: Seasonality and weather dependence concentrated in a single dominant product line

risks.note: The BRSR materiality table frames product quality and safety as 'non-negotiable': customers embed stringent quality specifications, dimensional tolerances and reliability standards in supply agreements, and 'failure to consistently meet these standards results in rejections, chargebacks, and ultimately, delisting from approved vendor lists.' Because Amber is a B2B contract manufacturer with no consumer brand of its own, the customer relationship IS the franchise - quality performance is described as 'the primary differentiator in vendor selection and long-term contract retention.' The same exposure runs through ESG: OEM customers embedding Scope 3 emissions tracking and supplier carbon criteria could put approved-vendor status at risk if credible climate action cannot be demonstrated, and compliance failures by supply chain partners can cause disqualification by ESG-conscious customers.
risks.risk: OEM/ODM customer dependence - quality or delivery failure means loss of approved-vendor status, not just a penalty

risks.note: Management lists 'Commodity Price and Currency Fluctuations' as a threat: short-term unpredictability in global prices of copper, aluminium and crude derivatives challenges operating margins, compounded by currency depreciation, and sustained cost inflation could itself change customer purchasing behaviour in price-sensitive segments. The BRSR supply-chain row adds that raw material price spikes 'can significantly compress gross margins if not adequately managed through procurement strategy or contractual pass-through mechanisms with customers' - i.e. pass-through is a mechanism to be negotiated, not a given. The exposure is amplified by the business model: consolidated Operating EBITDA margin is disclosed at 8.0% and net profit margin at 1.9%, so a small input-cost shock consumes a large share of profit.
risks.risk: Commodity price and currency volatility against structurally thin margins

risks.note: Procurement risk is the longest entry in the risk-management table, spanning commodity price volatility, currency depreciation, inflationary cost pressures, trade policy uncertainty, geopolitical and regional instability, global supply chain disruptions and critical component availability. The BRSR row is blunter still: import dependency for certain specialty inputs adds foreign exchange and logistics risk, and 'concentration risk from sole source or limited source supply arrangements for critical inputs amplifies vulnerability to disruption.' The consequence is asymmetric because OEM customers run just-in-time inventory - a supply failure at Amber 'translates rapidly into customer line stoppages and contractual penalties.' Mitigations cited are supplier diversification and qualified alternates, safety stock for long-lead inputs, supplier financial and compliance assessment, and a digital procurement platform.
risks.risk: Multi-tier supply chain concentration, import dependence and geopolitical disruption

risks.note: 'Coping with Changing Technology' is a named risk: rapid technological advancement and evolving product requirements may require continuous portfolio realignment, and the threats section warns that existing products, processes or capabilities may become 'less competitive over time.' This bites hardest in the Electronics pivot, where the company is simultaneously moving into multi-layer and HDI PCB manufacturing - technologies it does not yet operate at scale - and into industrial automation and power electronics through acquired entities. R&D is explicitly framed in the BRSR as the difference between being 'a development partner rather than a commodity supplier', so under-investment compresses both pricing and programme wins. Regulatory technology transitions compound this: the HFC phase-down roadmap for high-GWP refrigerants and tightening BEE energy-efficiency norms (revised Star Labelling effective January 2026) force product redesign on an externally set clock.
risks.risk: Technology obsolescence and the cost of staying qualified as capability moves up the value chain

risks.note: In one year the group added 7 manufacturing facilities (3 via acquisition), took majority stakes in Power-One (60%), Shogini Technoarts (80%) and Israel-listed Unitronics (40.2% rising to 50.4%), merged Ever Electronics into IL JIN, and committed to ECMS-approved investment plans of Rs 991 Crore (Ascent Circuits), Rs 3,215 Crore (Ascent-K) and Rs 500 Crore (Shogini), all funded partly by an approximately Rs 1,000 Crore QIP and approximately Rs 1,750 Crore raised at IL JIN. Every one of the three major planned expansions is described only as 'expected to become operational in the coming periods' with no commissioning date, and the Yujin JV plant is built but cannot produce until RDSO approvals arrive - a regulatory gate outside the company's control. That capital-at-risk is not hypothetical: reported PAT fell year-on-year because of an exceptional one-off impairment of the investment (including loan) in Shivaliks Mercantile plus the share of JV loss, and Sidwal exited that 49% joint venture entirely on 30 March 2026.
risks.risk: Execution and integration risk across a rapid acquisition and greenfield capex programme - with a realised loss already on the record

risks.note: Management describes the government's policy framework as 'a key catalyst of our expansion plan.' The three largest committed projects rest on approvals under the Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme, whose outlay was itself only raised from Rs 22,919 Crore to Rs 40,000 Crore in the Union Budget 2026-27, and the RAC value-addition thesis (20-25% rising to 75-80%) rests on the PLI scheme for white goods. Demand assumptions lean the same way - the GST cut on RACs from 28% to 18% effective September 2025, record Railway capex of Rs 2.93 lakh crore, defence indigenisation. Scheme conditions, disbursement timing or a change in policy priority would therefore hit both the return on the capex already committed and the demand pull assumed behind it.
risks.risk: Dependence on government policy schemes for the economics of the expansion plan

risks.note: Management flags 'Market Competition' - pressure from both well-established players and new entrants demanding continuous innovation and strategic positioning. Two structural workforce exposures sit alongside it in the BRSR data. First, of 14,023 workers only 2,379 are permanent, with 11,644 other-than-permanent; total workforce is 21,000+ including contractual labour, so a large share of manufacturing capacity depends on contract labour whose availability and cost are outside the payroll. Second, turnover is high - permanent employee turnover of 25.26% in FY2025-26 (32.49% in FY2024-25), which for a business whose moat is described as R&D and process capability is a retention risk on the very capability being built. The one-off provision of Rs 9 Crore on account of the New Labour Code shows the cost of labour-regulation change flowing straight to reported profit.
risks.risk: Competitive intensity and a largely contractual workforce with high turnover

currentContext.expansion: Amber's FY2025-26 expansion story is overwhelmingly an Electronics-division story funded partly by two capital raises (approximately Rs 1,000 Crore QIP at the parent and approximately Rs 1,750 Crore of CCPS and equity at IL JIN Electronics). As on 31st March 2026 the Company and its group entities collectively operate 37 manufacturing facilities across India and internationally, of which 16 are operated directly by the Company and 21 by subsidiaries and group entities. During the year 7 new manufacturing facilities were added, including 3 acquired through acquisitions, while certain existing facilities were consolidated or discontinued and two units (at Plot No. 36, Sector 31, Kasna Industrial Area, Site-IV, Greater Noida and one further industrial plot) were relocated to other operational facilities as part of ongoing operational optimisation. Three major planned expansions are under implementation and 'expected to become operational in the coming periods': IL JIN Electronics is expanding its PCB Assembly unit at Gat No. 160-2 and 164-2, Pimple Jagtap Road, Bhima Koregaon, Tal. Shirur, Pune, Maharashtra; Ascent Circuits is building a Multi-Layer PCB unit at Plot No. 8, ELCOSEZ, Viswanthapuram, Hosur, Krishnagiri District, Tamil Nadu, where construction is progressing well, backed by an ECMS-approved investment plan of Rs 991 Crore; and Ascent-K Circuit (a JV with Korea Circuit) is building an HDI PCB unit at Plot No. 4, Sector 10, EMC 2.0, YEIDA near Jewar Airport, Gautam Buddha Nagar, Uttar Pradesh, on a 16-acre site, backed by an ECMS-approved investment plan of Rs 3,215 Crore, with the ground-breaking ceremony held in June 2026. Shogini Technoarts separately secured ECMS approval for a multi-layer PCB investment plan of Rs 500 Crore. Growth also came inorganically through IL JIN: a 60% majority stake in Bengaluru-based Power-One Micro Systems (power electronics - BESS, solar inverters, EV chargers, industrial UPS) in August 2025 under definitive agreements dated 27th June 2025; an 80% stake in Maharashtra-based PCB maker Shogini Technoarts in December 2025 (adding single-sided, double-sided, multi-layer, metal-clad and flex PCB capability); and a stake in Israel-listed Unitronics built from an initial 40.2% in October 2025 to 49.7% by year-end and 50.4% in April 2026, giving majority ownership and access to HMI, PLC, variable frequency drive and industrial-automation software. In Consumer Durables the Company augmented Room AC manufacturing capacity at Sri City, Andhra Pradesh during the year and expanded the Light Commercial AC portfolio (inverter ductable range, One-Way Cassette ACs). In Railway Subsystems & Defence, Sidwal's new greenfield facility is expected to significantly strengthen manufacturing capacity, and the Yujin Machinery joint-venture facility is ready with commercial production expected to commence upon securing the requisite RDSO approvals. On the sustainability side the climate action strategy includes expansion of on-site solar power capacity and evaluation of Power Purchase Agreements for green electricity, though no megawatt figure is given. Beyond the three named planned expansions, no commissioning dates, capacity additions in product units, or rupee capex quantum for the group as a whole are disclosed anywhere in this bundle.

risks.risk: Seasonality and weather dependence concentrated in a single dominant product line
risks.note: Management names 'Seasonality Risk' explicitly: the Room AC segment is highly seasonal and vulnerable to volatile and unpredictable weather patterns, and 'unexpected shifts in weather patterns, fluctuating temperatures, or irregular seasonal changes make it challenging for air conditioning businesses to predict consumer demand accurately... leading to volatility in product sales and inventory misalignment.' This is not theoretical - the Directors' Report concedes FY2025-26 demand 'got adversely impacted owing to weather conditions' and the RAC industry stayed largely flattish. With Consumer Durables at 69% of divisional revenue and air conditioners and components accounting for over 90% of standalone turnover per BRSR, one weather season can swing the majority of the group. The stated mitigation is structural rather than operational - diversifying the mix into Electronics and Railway Subsystems & Defence to reduce dependence on RAC seasonality.

risks.risk: OEM/ODM customer dependence - quality or delivery failure means loss of approved-vendor status, not just a penalty
risks.note: The BRSR materiality table frames product quality and safety as 'non-negotiable': customers embed stringent quality specifications, dimensional tolerances and reliability standards in supply agreements, and 'failure to consistently meet these standards results in rejections, chargebacks, and ultimately, delisting from approved vendor lists.' Because Amber is a B2B contract manufacturer with no consumer brand of its own, the customer relationship IS the franchise - quality performance is described as 'the primary differentiator in vendor selection and long-term contract retention.' The same exposure runs through ESG: OEM customers embedding Scope 3 emissions tracking and supplier carbon criteria could put approved-vendor status at risk if credible climate action cannot be demonstrated, and compliance failures by supply chain partners can cause disqualification by ESG-conscious customers.

risks.risk: Commodity price and currency volatility against structurally thin margins
risks.note: Management lists 'Commodity Price and Currency Fluctuations' as a threat: short-term unpredictability in global prices of copper, aluminium and crude derivatives challenges operating margins, compounded by currency depreciation, and sustained cost inflation could itself change customer purchasing behaviour in price-sensitive segments. The BRSR supply-chain row adds that raw material price spikes 'can significantly compress gross margins if not adequately managed through procurement strategy or contractual pass-through mechanisms with customers' - i.e. pass-through is a mechanism to be negotiated, not a given. The exposure is amplified by the business model: consolidated Operating EBITDA margin is disclosed at 8.0% and net profit margin at 1.9%, so a small input-cost shock consumes a large share of profit.

risks.risk: Multi-tier supply chain concentration, import dependence and geopolitical disruption
risks.note: Procurement risk is the longest entry in the risk-management table, spanning commodity price volatility, currency depreciation, inflationary cost pressures, trade policy uncertainty, geopolitical and regional instability, global supply chain disruptions and critical component availability. The BRSR row is blunter still: import dependency for certain specialty inputs adds foreign exchange and logistics risk, and 'concentration risk from sole source or limited source supply arrangements for critical inputs amplifies vulnerability to disruption.' The consequence is asymmetric because OEM customers run just-in-time inventory - a supply failure at Amber 'translates rapidly into customer line stoppages and contractual penalties.' Mitigations cited are supplier diversification and qualified alternates, safety stock for long-lead inputs, supplier financial and compliance assessment, and a digital procurement platform.

risks.risk: Technology obsolescence and the cost of staying qualified as capability moves up the value chain
risks.note: 'Coping with Changing Technology' is a named risk: rapid technological advancement and evolving product requirements may require continuous portfolio realignment, and the threats section warns that existing products, processes or capabilities may become 'less competitive over time.' This bites hardest in the Electronics pivot, where the company is simultaneously moving into multi-layer and HDI PCB manufacturing - technologies it does not yet operate at scale - and into industrial automation and power electronics through acquired entities. R&D is explicitly framed in the BRSR as the difference between being 'a development partner rather than a commodity supplier', so under-investment compresses both pricing and programme wins. Regulatory technology transitions compound this: the HFC phase-down roadmap for high-GWP refrigerants and tightening BEE energy-efficiency norms (revised Star Labelling effective January 2026) force product redesign on an externally set clock.

risks.risk: Execution and integration risk across a rapid acquisition and greenfield capex programme - with a realised loss already on the record
risks.note: In one year the group added 7 manufacturing facilities (3 via acquisition), took majority stakes in Power-One (60%), Shogini Technoarts (80%) and Israel-listed Unitronics (40.2% rising to 50.4%), merged Ever Electronics into IL JIN, and committed to ECMS-approved investment plans of Rs 991 Crore (Ascent Circuits), Rs 3,215 Crore (Ascent-K) and Rs 500 Crore (Shogini), all funded partly by an approximately Rs 1,000 Crore QIP and approximately Rs 1,750 Crore raised at IL JIN. Every one of the three major planned expansions is described only as 'expected to become operational in the coming periods' with no commissioning date, and the Yujin JV plant is built but cannot produce until RDSO approvals arrive - a regulatory gate outside the company's control. That capital-at-risk is not hypothetical: reported PAT fell year-on-year because of an exceptional one-off impairment of the investment (including loan) in Shivaliks Mercantile plus the share of JV loss, and Sidwal exited that 49% joint venture entirely on 30 March 2026.

risks.risk: Dependence on government policy schemes for the economics of the expansion plan
risks.note: Management describes the government's policy framework as 'a key catalyst of our expansion plan.' The three largest committed projects rest on approvals under the Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme, whose outlay was itself only raised from Rs 22,919 Crore to Rs 40,000 Crore in the Union Budget 2026-27, and the RAC value-addition thesis (20-25% rising to 75-80%) rests on the PLI scheme for white goods. Demand assumptions lean the same way - the GST cut on RACs from 28% to 18% effective September 2025, record Railway capex of Rs 2.93 lakh crore, defence indigenisation. Scheme conditions, disbursement timing or a change in policy priority would therefore hit both the return on the capex already committed and the demand pull assumed behind it.

risks.risk: Competitive intensity and a largely contractual workforce with high turnover
risks.note: Management flags 'Market Competition' - pressure from both well-established players and new entrants demanding continuous innovation and strategic positioning. Two structural workforce exposures sit alongside it in the BRSR data. First, of 14,023 workers only 2,379 are permanent, with 11,644 other-than-permanent; total workforce is 21,000+ including contractual labour, so a large share of manufacturing capacity depends on contract labour whose availability and cost are outside the payroll. Second, turnover is high - permanent employee turnover of 25.26% in FY2025-26 (32.49% in FY2024-25), which for a business whose moat is described as R&D and process capability is a retention risk on the very capability being built. The one-off provision of Rs 9 Crore on account of the New Labour Code shows the cost of labour-regulation change flowing straight to reported profit.

one-line thesis: Amber enters India's mobile-phone market — the world's 2nd largest — via an **asset-light sublease of an existing Oppo India facility** (covers Oppo, OnePlus, Realme of the BBK group), targeting ~8M units in Year 1 (FY28) and 13–15M in Year 2 (FY29). Initial EBITDA is thin (industry 1.5–2% ex-PLI) but the play is **scale + ROCE (>30–35% standalone, 4–10 day working capital) now, then backward integration** into HDI-PCBs and other components (where margins are 15–16%) over 5–6 years — explicitly modeled on how Amber added components to ACs over 25 years to reach ~70% BOM. Also diversifies revenue and cuts the seasonal concentration of the RAC business.

guidance (critical — verify next quarter:
- **Timeline:** trial production **Q4 FY27**; commercial production **Q1 FY28**. First 3 months = learning curve (why the deliberately slow Q4FY27 start).
- **Volumes:** ~**8M units** (management: 8–9M; take 8M conservatively) in Year 1 = FY28 → **13–15M units** (14–15M conservative) in Year 2 = FY29. Represents ~20–30% of Oppo India's volume.
- **Margin:** at commencement in line with industry (~1.5–2% EBITDA ex-PLI); improves as operating scale + local value addition rise.
- **Local value addition:** start assembly + SMT (industry today only ~10–12%, "everybody doing only assembly"); **add HDI PCBs in Year 2**; then progressively raise local value addition to **35–40% over the next 5–6 years** (mgmt also said "30–35%" — road map not yet formalized).
- **Capex:** **<₹50cr** for assembly + SMT to start (asset-light sublease). Component-line capex only after 14–15M units is reached; PCB capex already underway (no duplication).
- **ROCE:** mobile vertical **>30–35% on a standalone basis**; ROCE-accretive to group. PCB/component margins 15–16%.
order book & pipeline:
- Committed ramp: ~8M units Yr1 (FY28) → 13–15M units Yr2 (FY29), across 3 BBK brands (Oppo, OnePlus, Realme).
- Long-term relationship framing — "beginning of a longer relationship with Oppo"; will explore additional avenues (incl. **supplying components** to Oppo/its other EMS partners over time).
- Vivo: no arrangement. BBK-group brands beyond the three: not committed; "baby steps" first.
segment / subsidiary detail:
- **Existing scale base (capability proof):** IL JIN makes **9–10M smart watches/yr** and **~15M PCB assemblies/yr**; AC business does **~5.5M boxes/yr**. Assembly scale "not a problem at all."
- **Ascent Circuits:** Amber raised stake from 60% → **98.5%**. Founder-MD Mr. Manjunath stepped down (no longer a shareholder). **PCB division now headed by Mr. Santosh** (25 yrs PCB experience, ex-AT&S — formerly the largest PCB company; with Amber ~1 year). "Amber has become the largest PCB company" with Ascent + Shogini.
- **Mobile entity structure undecided** — will sit either directly under Amber or under IL JIN (IL JIN has minority shareholders on its cap table); decision before commencement of operations.
- A **dedicated senior-most management team** will run the mobile vertical (separate from wearables/hearables).
growth verticals / optionality:
- **Backward integration ladder:** assembly + SMT → HDI interconnect PCBs (Yr2) → then one component every ~year (candidates named: camera modules, displays, metal casings, chargers) over 5–6 years.
- **Component margin pool** (15–16% on PCB; "decent" across the mobile component ecosystem) is the real prize vs. thin assembly margins.
- Oppo to help **bring more component suppliers to India** — ecosystem build-out for local value addition.
- **AC analogy as template:** over 25 yrs Amber went sheet-metal → assembly → heat exchangers → injection molding → motor company → inverter PCB → fans & boards, reaching ~70% of BOM. Same "balance volume and value play" intended for mobile.
margins & cost dynamics:
- Assembly-only EBITDA structurally thin: industry ~1.5–2% ex-PLI; higher-end models ~1.5–1.7%, lower-end models a higher %.
- Deal economics sit on the **bottom line, not the top line** — Amber has flexibility whether a model is booked gross (ODM-style) or on job-work value-add; absolute profit is protected either way (per Oppo India's choice, model by model).
- Margin expansion is entirely a **mix/value-addition story** — SMT, then HDI/PCB (15–16%), then further components.
capex / expansion (watch slippage):
- **Assembly + SMT: <₹50cr** total to start (sublease → no facility capex; "very, very minimal").
- **No Press Note 3 approval required** (sublease of an existing Oppo facility) — removes a regulatory timeline risk.
- **Component capex deferred** to after 14–15M units; magnitude depends on which components (camera modules / display / metal casings). PCB capex already in progress → **no duplication**.
- On an "eventual investment" question (multiples of ₹1,000cr vs ₹200cr), mgmt declined a number — reiterated <₹50cr near-term and component capex sized later.
capital allocation:
- Asset-light, low-working-capital (4–5 days, max 10) → structurally high, improving ROCE (mobile >30–35% standalone).
- Consistent with stated strategy: **balance high-margin value-add businesses with asset-light, high-volume, low-margin businesses**.
- No equity dilution flagged for the initial phase; Ascent stake step-up (to 98.5%) already funded.
risks & watch-items:
- **Execution / learning curve** — ramping to ~8M units after a 3-month learning period; first commercial output only Q1FY28 (slippage risk).
- **Thin margins** amplify any operational inefficiency; profitability hinges on the still-unformalized backward-integration road map landing on schedule.
- **Flat domestic phone TAM** — total units sold in India roughly flat for 4–5 years; growth comes from ASP/premiumization and local-value-addition share, not unit growth. Amber "beats its TAM" within ~2 years at 15M, so the endless-TAM claim rests entirely on climbing the value chain.
- **PLI uncertainty** — a revised (2nd) PLI is only speculated (value-addition-led); no draft yet; mgmt declined to model it.
- **Single-customer dependency** on Oppo India volume stability; entity/accounting structure (gross vs job-work; Amber vs IL JIN) still undecided.
management quality / tone: Measured and disciplined — repeated "baby steps," a 3-month learning-curve buffer, and conservative volume framing (take 8M not 9M; 14–15M not "maybe more"). Credibility anchored in the demonstrated wearables scale-up (0→10M watches in ~4 years) and the 25-year AC backward-integration track record. Notably principled on ecosystem conduct: explicitly **asked Oppo not to hand it other EMS players' existing business** ("that is not Amber's model"). Declined to speculate on PLI structure or eventual capex numbers without hard data.
non-obvious takeaways:
- The **sublease structure sidesteps Press Note 3** approval — a meaningful timeline/regulatory advantage over a fresh-facility entry.
- Revenue-recognition is deliberately **flexible (gross vs job-work) with protected absolute profit** — so reported "revenue" from this vertical may be optically large or small without changing the P&L contribution; watch how it's disclosed.
- Amber quietly consolidated to become "the **largest PCB company**" (Ascent 98.5% + Shogini) with an ex-AT&S leader — the PCB/HDI backbone that makes the mobile-component margin story credible pre-exists the Oppo deal.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Amber is a diversified, backward-integrated B2B (OEM/ODM) manufacturing solutions provider operating 37 manufacturing facilities across Consumer Durables, Electronics and Railway Subsystems & Defence, having evolved from a Room Air Conditioner specialist into a multi-industry contract manufacturer.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Amber Enterprises India Limited, together with its subsidiaries and joint ventures (the 'Amber Group'), makes finished products and components for other brands rather than selling under its own consumer brand. In Consumer Durables it supplies Complete Built Units (CBUs) of Room and Commercial Air Conditioners plus a wide range of RAC and non-RAC components (heat exchangers, motors, multi-flow condensers, copper tubing, sheet metal, plastic extrusion, vacuum forming and injection moulding, refrigerator case liners, washing-machine tub assemblies) to leading MNC and domestic appliance brands. The Electronics Division supplies EMS (PCB assembly and box build), bare PCBs, power electronics and industrial automation solutions to consumer electronics, automotive, telecom, aerospace and defence, energy and industrial customers, while the Railway Subsystems & Defence Division (through Sidwal) supplies HVAC systems, rolling-stock subsystems and precision cooling to railways, metros, RRTS, buses and defence. Revenue split by division in FY2025-26 was 69% Consumer Durables, 27% Electronics and 4% Railway Subsystems & Defence.

guidance.title: Guidance (CRITICAL — verify next quarter)
guidance.body:
- **Timeline:** trial production **Q4 FY27**; commercial production **Q1 FY28**. First 3 months = learning curve (why the deliberately slow Q4FY27 start).
- **Volumes:** ~**8M units** (management: 8–9M; take 8M conservatively) in Year 1 = FY28 → **13–15M units** (14–15M conservative) in Year 2 = FY29. Represents ~20–30% of Oppo India's volume.
- **Margin:** at commencement in line with industry (~1.5–2% EBITDA ex-PLI); improves as operating scale + local value addition rise.
- **Local value addition:** start assembly + SMT (industry today only ~10–12%, "everybody doing only assembly"); **add HDI PCBs in Year 2**; then progressively raise local value addition to **35–40% over the next 5–6 years** (mgmt also said "30–35%" — road map not yet formalized).
- **Capex:** **<₹50cr** for assembly + SMT to start (asset-light sublease). Component-line capex only after 14–15M units is reached; PCB capex already underway (no duplication).
- **ROCE:** mobile vertical **>30–35% on a standalone basis**; ROCE-accretive to group. PCB/component margins 15–16%.

growth_optionality.title: Growth verticals / optionality
growth_optionality.body:
- **Backward integration ladder:** assembly + SMT → HDI interconnect PCBs (Yr2) → then one component every ~year (candidates named: camera modules, displays, metal casings, chargers) over 5–6 years.
- **Component margin pool** (15–16% on PCB; "decent" across the mobile component ecosystem) is the real prize vs. thin assembly margins.
- Oppo to help **bring more component suppliers to India** — ecosystem build-out for local value addition.
- **AC analogy as template:** over 25 yrs Amber went sheet-metal → assembly → heat exchangers → injection molding → motor company → inverter PCB → fans & boards, reaching ~70% of BOM. Same "balance volume and value play" intended for mobile.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- RAC household penetration in India is around 12%, materially below comparable Asian markets - management frames this as a multi-decade runway and 'visible headroom'
- GST on Room Air Conditioners was cut from 28% to 18% effective September 2025, which management expects to enhance affordability, support first-time adoption among price-sensitive consumers and improve access to premium 5-star models
- Rising ambient temperatures, extended summer seasons and more frequent heatwaves are shifting cooling from a discretionary luxury to a necessity, accelerating both first-time adoption and the replacement cycle, and lengthening the seasonal selling window
- Middle-class expansion - middle-class and affluent consumers are expected to account for 93% of total consumer spending by 2036; households in the upper-middle and high income bands are projected to rise sharply by 2030/31
- Urbanisation - India's urban population grew from roughly 31% in 2011 to roughly 36% in 2025 and is projected to exceed 40% by 2030, with housing-society expansion in Tier II and III cities driving RAC installations
- Per capita GDP rising from about US$ 2,591 in 2024 to a projected US$ 2,812 by 2026 and US$ 4,047 by 2030, crossing the affordability threshold for first-time and multi-room air conditioning
- PLI Scheme for white goods expected to bring cumulative investment of Rs 11,198 Crore across the value chain, with domestic value addition targeted to rise from 20-25% to 75-80%
- BEE revised Star Labelling standards implemented January 2026 mandate higher energy-performance benchmarks, strengthening demand for energy-efficient RACs and, by implication, for redesigned components
- FY2025-26 RAC demand was adversely impacted by non-conducive weather, but management insists the structural fundamentals remain firmly intact - an explicit demand-timing versus demand-structure distinction
- ESDM/EMS is maturing from pure assembly towards component engineering and value-added activity, with Indian manufacturers pushing import substitution and deeper local value addition
- ECMS outlay increased from an initial Rs 22,919 Crore to Rs 40,000 Crore in the Union Budget 2026-27, expected to attract investment commitments exceeding Rs 1.15 lakh crore, generate production worth over Rs 10 lakh crore and create more than 1.4 lakh direct jobs
- Rising electronics content per product and the growth of smart and connected devices expands EMS demand across sectors
- Automotive electronics and the EV ecosystem structurally increase electronic content per vehicle (telematics, connectivity, security, infotainment, powertrain electrification); rigorous qualification protocols create a high entry threshold that favours incumbents
- Digitalisation, cloud computing, digital services and data centres drive demand for electronic hardware, networking equipment and power management solutions
- Bare PCBs remain substantially import-dependent, which management presents as the localisation opportunity behind the Ascent/Ascent-K/Shogini investments
- Indian Railways allocated a record capital expenditure of Rs 2.93 lakh crore, with seven new high-speed rail corridors planned and continued Vande Bharat and Amrit Bharat deployment
- Vande Bharat Sleeper and Metro variants have more demanding climate-control requirements, driving higher technological complexity and higher value per coach in rail HVAC
- India's operational metro network crossed the 1,000-km milestone across 11 states and 23 cities - third largest in the world - with Metro and RRTS expansion across more than 20 cities unlocking multi-year subsystem demand
- Public-private partnership models in station redevelopment, rolling stock and logistics, alongside Make in India localisation, are broadening the addressable rail market
- Margin lever cited: operating EBITDA growth driven by improved operating performance and a favourable shift towards higher-margin products
- Mix lever cited: Consumer Durables provides a strong and growing baseline while the strategic shift towards electronics and mobility-led segments progressively reshapes the composition of the business
- Management's stated view is that manufacturers with integrated capabilities, strong technology partnerships and diversified product portfolios are best positioned to benefit from the shift to value-added electronics manufacturing - a self-description of Amber's positioning
- Railway Subsystems & Defence Division: 'The Division continued to witness encouraging momentum across the Railway, Metro, and Defence segments, supported by an expanding product portfolio and healthy order book visibility.'
- Chairman's statement on the same division: 'With a healthy order book and an expanding product portfolio, we remain optimistic about the strong growth prospects of this Division.'
- Railways outlook: 'With a broadening product portfolio and ramping offtake of products, the Company is strongly positioned to drive sustainable future growth.'
- No order-book value, tenure or book-to-bill figure is disclosed anywhere in this bundle - the mentions are qualitative only, and are confined to the Railway Subsystems & Defence Division

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body:
- Assembly-only EBITDA structurally thin: industry ~1.5–2% ex-PLI; higher-end models ~1.5–1.7%, lower-end models a higher %.
- Deal economics sit on the **bottom line, not the top line** — Amber has flexibility whether a model is booked gross (ODM-style) or on job-work value-add; absolute profit is protected either way (per Oppo India's choice, model by model).
- Margin expansion is entirely a **mix/value-addition story** — SMT, then HDI/PCB (15–16%), then further components.

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Asset-light, low-working-capital (4–5 days, max 10) → structurally high, improving ROCE (mobile >30–35% standalone).
- Consistent with stated strategy: **balance high-margin value-add businesses with asset-light, high-volume, low-margin businesses**.
- No equity dilution flagged for the initial phase; Ascent stake step-up (to 98.5%) already funded.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Amber's FY2025-26 expansion story is overwhelmingly an Electronics-division story funded partly by two capital raises (approximately Rs 1,000 Crore QIP at the parent and approximately Rs 1,750 Crore of CCPS and equity at IL JIN Electronics). As on 31st March 2026 the Company and its group entities collectively operate 37 manufacturing facilities across India and internationally, of which 16 are operated directly by the Company and 21 by subsidiaries and group entities. During the year 7 new manufacturing facilities were added, including 3 acquired through acquisitions, while certain existing facilities were consolidated or discontinued and two units (at Plot No. 36, Sector 31, Kasna Industrial Area, Site-IV, Greater Noida and one further industrial plot) were relocated to other operational facilities as part of ongoing operational optimisation. Three major planned expansions are under implementation and 'expected to become operational in the coming periods': IL JIN Electronics is expanding its PCB Assembly unit at Gat No. 160-2 and 164-2, Pimple Jagtap Road, Bhima Koregaon, Tal. Shirur, Pune, Maharashtra; Ascent Circuits is building a Multi-Layer PCB unit at Plot No. 8, ELCOSEZ, Viswanthapuram, Hosur, Krishnagiri District, Tamil Nadu, where construction is progressing well, backed by an ECMS-approved investment plan of Rs 991 Crore; and Ascent-K Circuit (a JV with Korea Circuit) is building an HDI PCB unit at Plot No. 4, Sector 10, EMC 2.0, YEIDA near Jewar Airport, Gautam Buddha Nagar, Uttar Pradesh, on a 16-acre site, backed by an ECMS-approved investment plan of Rs 3,215 Crore, with the ground-breaking ceremony held in June 2026. Shogini Technoarts separately secured ECMS approval for a multi-layer PCB investment plan of Rs 500 Crore. Growth also came inorganically through IL JIN: a 60% majority stake in Bengaluru-based Power-One Micro Systems (power electronics - BESS, solar inverters, EV chargers, industrial UPS) in August 2025 under definitive agreements dated 27th June 2025; an 80% stake in Maharashtra-based PCB maker Shogini Technoarts in December 2025 (adding single-sided, double-sided, multi-layer, metal-clad and flex PCB capability); and a stake in Israel-listed Unitronics built from an initial 40.2% in October 2025 to 49.7% by year-end and 50.4% in April 2026, giving majority ownership and access to HMI, PLC, variable frequency drive and industrial-automation software. In Consumer Durables the Company augmented Room AC manufacturing capacity at Sri City, Andhra Pradesh during the year and expanded the Light Commercial AC portfolio (inverter ductable range, One-Way Cassette ACs). In Railway Subsystems & Defence, Sidwal's new greenfield facility is expected to significantly strengthen manufacturing capacity, and the Yujin Machinery joint-venture facility is ready with commercial production expected to commence upon securing the requisite RDSO approvals. On the sustainability side the climate action strategy includes expansion of on-site solar power capacity and evaluation of Power Purchase Agreements for green electricity, though no megawatt figure is given. Beyond the three named planned expansions, no commissioning dates, capacity additions in product units, or rupee capex quantum for the group as a whole are disclosed anywhere in this bundle.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Measured and disciplined — repeated "baby steps," a 3-month learning-curve buffer, and conservative volume framing (take 8M not 9M; 14–15M not "maybe more"). Credibility anchored in the demonstrated wearables scale-up (0→10M watches in ~4 years) and the 25-year AC backward-integration track record. Notably principled on ecosystem conduct: explicitly **asked Oppo not to hand it other EMS players' existing business** ("that is not Amber's model"). Declined to speculate on PLI structure or eventual capex numbers without hard data.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Deep backward integration in the RAC value chain built over three decades - described as one of the most backward-integrated players in the Room Air Conditioner industry, giving deep manufacturing capability and cost competitiveness
- Breadth of the component portfolio across sheet metal, plastics, copper tubing, motors and heat exchangers, so a customer can source both CBUs and components from one partner
- Diversification across three divisions with materially different demand cycles - Consumer Durables 69%, Electronics 27%, Railway Subsystems & Defence 4% of FY26 revenue - which cushioned a weather-hit RAC year
- Pan-India footprint of 37 facilities across 10 states providing scale, flexibility and proximity to key customers
- R&D strength of 370+ employees supporting product development and ODM capability
- Long-standing OEM/ODM relationships with leading MNC and domestic brands; positioned as a 'trusted manufacturing partner' with high qualification thresholds in automotive and defence electronics
- Ability to consolidate the electronics component chain through acquisition - Power-One (power electronics), Shogini (bare PCB), Unitronics (industrial automation), Ascent/Ascent-K (multi-layer and HDI PCB)
- Policy tailwind capture - ECMS approvals secured by three group entities, and PLI participation in white goods
- Sidwal's recognised position in railway/metro HVAC with a pan-India service network and an expanding content-per-coach product portfolio (doors, gangways, couplers, pantographs, brakes)
- Balance-sheet capacity refreshed during FY26 through an approximately Rs 1,000 Crore QIP at the parent and approximately Rs 1,750 Crore of CCPS/equity funding raised at IL JIN Electronics
- Strong external credit standing - ICRA short-term rating of A1+ at the parent, and [ICRA]AA- (Stable)/A1+ at IL JIN and Ascent, CRISIL AA-/Positive at Sidwal

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body:
- **Execution / learning curve** — ramping to ~8M units after a 3-month learning period; first commercial output only Q1FY28 (slippage risk).
- **Thin margins** amplify any operational inefficiency; profitability hinges on the still-unformalized backward-integration road map landing on schedule.
- **Flat domestic phone TAM** — total units sold in India roughly flat for 4–5 years; growth comes from ASP/premiumization and local-value-addition share, not unit growth. Amber "beats its TAM" within ~2 years at 15M, so the endless-TAM claim rests entirely on climbing the value chain.
- **PLI uncertainty** — a revised (2nd) PLI is only speculated (value-addition-led); no draft yet; mgmt declined to model it.
- **Single-customer dependency** on Oppo India volume stability; entity/accounting structure (gross vs job-work; Amber vs IL JIN) still undecided.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body:
- The **sublease structure sidesteps Press Note 3** approval — a meaningful timeline/regulatory advantage over a fresh-facility entry.
- Revenue-recognition is deliberately **flexible (gross vs job-work) with protected absolute profit** — so reported "revenue" from this vertical may be optically large or small without changing the P&L contribution; watch how it's disclosed.
- Amber quietly consolidated to become "the **largest PCB company**" (Ascent 98.5% + Shogini) with an ex-AT&S leader — the PCB/HDI backbone that makes the mobile-component margin story credible pre-exists the Oppo deal.
- Mgmt hints the relationship could **invert** over time — from Amber assembling Oppo phones to **Amber supplying components** to Oppo and even its other EMS partners.

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Three stated priorities for the next phase of growth: deepening backward integration, expanding manufacturing capabilities, and accelerating innovation-led growth through disciplined execution
- Diversify away from a single-product RAC dependency into Electronics and mobility-led segments, so that no one division's cycle (notably weather-driven RAC demand) dictates group performance
- Deepen backward integration in the RAC/Consumer Durables value chain, extending from CBUs into RAC and non-RAC components to hold cost competitiveness and wallet share with OEM customers
- Build the Electronics …

one-line thesis: Amber enters India's mobile-phone market — the world's 2nd largest — via an **asset-light sublease of an existing Oppo India facility** (covers Oppo, OnePlus, Realme of the BBK group), targeting ~8M units in Year 1 (FY28) and 13–15M in Year 2 (FY29). Initial EBITDA is thin (industry 1.5–2% ex-PLI) but the play is **scale + ROCE (>30–35% standalone, 4–10 day working capital) now, then backward integration** into HDI-PCBs and other components (where margins are 15–16%) over 5–6 years — explicitly modeled on how Amber added components to ACs over 25 years to reach ~70% BOM. Also diversifies revenue and cuts the seasonal concentration of the RAC business.

guidance (critical — verify next quarter:
- **Timeline:** trial production **Q4 FY27**; commercial production **Q1 FY28**. First 3 months = learning curve (why the deliberately slow Q4FY27 start).
- **Volumes:** ~**8M units** (management: 8–9M; take 8M conservatively) in Year 1 = FY28 → **13–15M units** (14–15M conservative) in Year 2 = FY29. Represents ~20–30% of Oppo India's volume.
- **Margin:** at commencement in line with industry (~1.5–2% EBITDA ex-PLI); improves as operating scale + local value addition rise.
- **Local value addition:** start assembly + SMT (industry today only ~10–12%, "everybody doing only assembly"); **add HDI PCBs in Year 2**; then progressively raise local value addition to **35–40% over the next 5–6 years** (mgmt also said "30–35%" — road map not yet formalized).
- **Capex:** **<₹50cr** for assembly + SMT to start (asset-light sublease). Component-line capex only after 14–15M units is reached; PCB capex already underway (no duplication).
- **ROCE:** mobile vertical **>30–35% on a standalone basis**; ROCE-accretive to group. PCB/component margins 15–16%.
order book & pipeline:
- Committed ramp: ~8M units Yr1 (FY28) → 13–15M units Yr2 (FY29), across 3 BBK brands (Oppo, OnePlus, Realme).
- Long-term relationship framing — "beginning of a longer relationship with Oppo"; will explore additional avenues (incl. **supplying components** to Oppo/its other EMS partners over time).
- Vivo: no arrangement. BBK-group brands beyond the three: not committed; "baby steps" first.
segment / subsidiary detail:
- **Existing scale base (capability proof):** IL JIN makes **9–10M smart watches/yr** and **~15M PCB assemblies/yr**; AC business does **~5.5M boxes/yr**. Assembly scale "not a problem at all."
- **Ascent Circuits:** Amber raised stake from 60% → **98.5%**. Founder-MD Mr. Manjunath stepped down (no longer a shareholder). **PCB division now headed by Mr. Santosh** (25 yrs PCB experience, ex-AT&S — formerly the largest PCB company; with Amber ~1 year). "Amber has become the largest PCB company" with Ascent + Shogini.
- **Mobile entity structure undecided** — will sit either directly under Amber or under IL JIN (IL JIN has minority shareholders on its cap table); decision before commencement of operations.
- A **dedicated senior-most management team** will run the mobile vertical (separate from wearables/hearables).
growth verticals / optionality:
- **Backward integration ladder:** assembly + SMT → HDI interconnect PCBs (Yr2) → then one component every ~year (candidates named: camera modules, displays, metal casings, chargers) over 5–6 years.
- **Component margin pool** (15–16% on PCB; "decent" across the mobile component ecosystem) is the real prize vs. thin assembly margins.
- Oppo to help **bring more component suppliers to India** — ecosystem build-out for local value addition.
- **AC analogy as template:** over 25 yrs Amber went sheet-metal → assembly → heat exchangers → injection molding → motor company → inverter PCB → fans & boards, reaching ~70% of BOM. Same "balance volume and value play" intended for mobile.
margins & cost dynamics:
- Assembly-only EBITDA structurally thin: industry ~1.5–2% ex-PLI; higher-end models ~1.5–1.7%, lower-end models a higher %.
- Deal economics sit on the **bottom line, not the top line** — Amber has flexibility whether a model is booked gross (ODM-style) or on job-work value-add; absolute profit is protected either way (per Oppo India's choice, model by model).
- Margin expansion is entirely a **mix/value-addition story** — SMT, then HDI/PCB (15–16%), then further components.
capex / expansion (watch slippage):
- **Assembly + SMT: <₹50cr** total to start (sublease → no facility capex; "very, very minimal").
- **No Press Note 3 approval required** (sublease of an existing Oppo facility) — removes a regulatory timeline risk.
- **Component capex deferred** to after 14–15M units; magnitude depends on which components (camera modules / display / metal casings). PCB capex already in progress → **no duplication**.
- On an "eventual investment" question (multiples of ₹1,000cr vs ₹200cr), mgmt declined a number — reiterated <₹50cr near-term and component capex sized later.
capital allocation:
- Asset-light, low-working-capital (4–5 days, max 10) → structurally high, improving ROCE (mobile >30–35% standalone).
- Consistent with stated strategy: **balance high-margin value-add businesses with asset-light, high-volume, low-margin businesses**.
- No equity dilution flagged for the initial phase; Ascent stake step-up (to 98.5%) already funded.
risks & watch-items:
- **Execution / learning curve** — ramping to ~8M units after a 3-month learning period; first commercial output only Q1FY28 (slippage risk).
- **Thin margins** amplify any operational inefficiency; profitability hinges on the still-unformalized backward-integration road map landing on schedule.
- **Flat domestic phone TAM** — total units sold in India roughly flat for 4–5 years; growth comes from ASP/premiumization and local-value-addition share, not unit growth. Amber "beats its TAM" within ~2 years at 15M, so the endless-TAM claim rests entirely on climbing the value chain.
- **PLI uncertainty** — a revised (2nd) PLI is only speculated (value-addition-led); no draft yet; mgmt declined to model it.
- **Single-customer dependency** on Oppo India volume stability; entity/accounting structure (gross vs job-work; Amber vs IL JIN) still undecided.
management quality / tone: Measured and disciplined — repeated "baby steps," a 3-month learning-curve buffer, and conservative volume framing (take 8M not 9M; 14–15M not "maybe more"). Credibility anchored in the demonstrated wearables scale-up (0→10M watches in ~4 years) and the 25-year AC backward-integration track record. Notably principled on ecosystem conduct: explicitly **asked Oppo not to hand it other EMS players' existing business** ("that is not Amber's model"). Declined to speculate on PLI structure or eventual capex numbers without hard data.
non-obvious takeaways:
- The **sublease structure sidesteps Press Note 3** approval — a meaningful timeline/regulatory advantage over a fresh-facility entry.
- Revenue-recognition is deliberately **flexible (gross vs job-work) with protected absolute profit** — so reported "revenue" from this vertical may be optically large or small without changing the P&L contribution; watch how it's disclosed.
- Amber quietly consolidated to become "the **largest PCB company**" (Ascent 98.5% + Shogini) with an ex-AT&S leader — the PCB/HDI backbone that makes the mobile-component margin story credible pre-exists the Oppo deal.
- Mgmt hints the relationship could **invert** over time — from Amber assembling Oppo phones to **Amber supplying components** to Oppo and even its other EMS partners.
